plants.name: Helianthus annuus
plants.description: Towering stalks crowned with huge golden-rayed flower heads that sweep across fields and roadsides, turning their faces toward the summer sun and humming with bees.
plants.location: North American prairies and plains, such as South Dakota, and gardens across the Northern Hemisphere
plants.funFact: A sunflower head is really hundreds of tiny flowers packed together. Each one becomes a seed, and the spiral patterns they form follow Fibonacci numbers.

plants.name: Echinacea purpurea
plants.description: Daisy-like blooms with drooping rose-purple petals around a spiky, copper-orange central cone. They are a favorite of butterflies and goldfinches in the high-summer prairie.
plants.location: Eastern and central North American prairies and gardens
plants.funFact: The spiky central cone gives the genus its name, from the Greek word for hedgehog. Goldfinches often feed on the seeds in late summer.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: South Africa's national flower is a giant, artichoke-like bloom ringed with pink, silky-tipped bracts. It is the largest of all the proteas and lights up the fynbos in the cool months.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mainly winter and spring, June to October
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western Cape, South Africa, including Kirstenbosch gardens
plants.funFact: Proteas belong to one of the oldest flowering plant families on Earth, and the genus is named for the shape-shifting Greek god Proteus.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Branches are smothered in fragrant, fluffy golden pom-pom flowers that brighten the late-winter Australian bush and draw in birds and bees.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to early spring, typically August and September
plants.funFact: Golden wattle is Australia's national floral emblem, and Wattle Day is celebrated every year on 1 September.
